where: the open modal, centred at x 448–992; both frames
finding: The two scenes that exist to answer J5 (the collision) and J6 (the link in flight) render a form with no sync state on it at all. On sync-editor, a save of last name + grade is supposedly still going, yet the form shows First name 'Ava', Last name 'Chen', Grade '9th grade' — the pre-edit values — every box live, 'Saved in Planning Center' under each one, and Save changes enabled. Dana opens the record she just edited, sees the old surname, retypes or re-saves, and queues a second job that overwrites her own in-flight correction. On sync-blocked the same form opens on Amara Whitfield, a quick-add with no upstream person, and tells the leader her name and grade are 'Saved in Planning Center', prefills birthday '14 March 2011 — already what Planning Center holds' and Ava's allergy text, and offers Save. That is a form inviting a write against a record that does not exist, on the codebase whose most-guarded failure is a duplicate child in the church's permanent database.
evidence: Each page carries two <dialog> elements. The first holds the designed content — 'Your last change is still saving / Last name and grade went to Planning Center 14 seconds ago. These boxes unlock as soon as it lands, so two edits cannot cross' and 'Amara is still being created in Planning Center / She was quick-added at the door 40 seconds ago … Notes are Tally's own and can be typed now' — with 17 disabled attributes on the managed controls. That dialog has no open attribute. The second dialog, marked open="" data-uxr-modal="", is a verbatim copy of the baseline editor with no sync content and nothing disabled, and it is the one that paints. sync-blocked--desktop-fold.png and sync-editor--desktop-fold.png are pixel-identical apart from the four words in the title bar and the two name fields.
direction: Move open="" onto the authored dialog in both files and delete the baseline duplicate, so the round can actually be judged. Two things to settle while doing it: the in-flight lock currently freezes all four managed fields for a job that only touched two, so Dana cannot add an allergy note while a surname is in flight — lock the fields the job names and leave the rest; and sync-blocked should carry the move the list chip already implies ('push them now') plus a statement that anything typed now rides along with the create rather than being retyped.

where: the row list, chip slot immediately right of the grade column (x ≈ 1150–1215)
finding: J2 is nine edits in four minutes and the question is 'which are done'. Nothing on this screen ever says done. A row whose edit landed forty seconds ago is byte-identical to the thirty-six rows Dana never touched — same name, same grade, no chip. So the absence of a chip means two opposite things, 'nothing was ever in flight' and 'it worked', and Dana cannot tell them apart without opening the record. After nine edits she either opens nine profiles to confirm, or trusts and does not check. Both are the outcomes this refinement exists to remove.
evidence: Across all 45 rows in sync-students--desktop-full.png only four chips exist: Saving (Ava, row 1), Waiting (Marcus, row 2), Needs you (Benson, row 3), Queued (Amara, row 10). There is no green present-token anywhere on the list, and no filter pill counts in-flight or recently-landed work — the three pills are Incomplete profiles 10, Needs you 1, Visitors 1. Rows are 44px pitch, 17 fit above the 900px fold, the page is 2199px, so 28 of the 45 rows are below it; nine edits scattered A–Z mean two full scrolls to survey a state that is not being reported anyway.
direction: A transient landed token in the same chip slot — 'Saved' in present green, decaying after a minute or two — costs nothing against the no-copy rule because it reports the job's outcome, not the value, and shows nothing new about a minor. Pair it with a session counter in the pill row ('3 in flight · 5 saved') so the survey is one glance at a fixed spot rather than a scroll down 2199px. There is also 500px of dead row between the end of the name (x≈500) and the last-seen column (x≈1010) on every one of the 45 rows — that is where who queued it and how long ago belong, and it is free.

where: Amara Whitfield's row (row 10), the grey 'Queued' chip at the far right, x ≈ 1345
finding: The screen uses the word 'Queued' for the one thing the brief's table says it does not mean, and has no word for the thing it does. Amara's chip title reads 'Waiting to be created in Planning Center' — that is a pending link, J6's case, not a queued edit. Meanwhile the state 'queued' (written down, no worker has claimed it, cancellable) has no representation on the list at all, so a leader scanning for their own just-pressed Save either sees nothing or reads Amara's grey chip and believes an edit is sitting on her. It is also styled as a permanent attribute: bg-ink-800 / text-ink-300 with hover:brightness, the exact treatment as 'No contact' and 'No birthday' two chips to its left, so it reads as a category the student belongs to rather than a clock that is running.
evidence: sync-students--desktop-full.png row 10: 'Visitor' (brand), 'No contact' (ink-800), 'Queued' (ink-800) sit in one right-aligned cluster. The three real job chips — Saving, Waiting, Needs you — use warn/danger with a ◷ or ⚠ glyph and sit in a different, fixed slot right after the grade. So the four chips a leader has to read as job state are split across two columns in two visual languages.
direction: Rename Amara's chip to what it is ('Not in PCO yet' / 'Creating…') and put a real queued token in the job slot, distinct from Saving — the brief's separation is written down and worth honouring: queued is cancellable, sending is not, and one chip that covers both makes the cancel affordance a coin toss.

where: the Saving and Waiting chips on rows 1 and 2, x ≈ 1150–1215, 11px text
finding: The chips carry no age and no explanation, so on a laptop three of the nine states collapse into two words that cannot be trusted. 'Saving' on a job fourteen seconds old and 'Saving' on a job four minutes old are the same pixels — stalled is not distinguishable from sending, and the brief says stalled must not read as failed because it may still land. 'Waiting' is worse: it means backed off on a rate limit and will resume on its own, and nothing on the screen says any of that. Dana sees an amber 'Waiting' sitting on Marcus's row through two minutes of a busy lobby kiosk, concludes it is stuck, and re-saves — a second write upstream for a correction that was already on its way.
evidence: Both chips are inert <span> elements: no title, no aria description, not focusable, no hover style. Every other chip in the same rows is a <button> with a title and hover:brightness-125 — 'Missing parent contact', 'Has allergies on file', 'Waiting to be created in Planning Center'. So the only chips that carry a live, time-sensitive, ambiguous state are the only ones a pointer cannot interrogate, on the one viewport where hover is free.
direction: Age belongs in the chip on desktop, where there is room for it — 'Saving 14s', and the same token turning to a stalled wording past ~2 min with the words 'still may land'. Give the job chips the hover the data chips already have: a title on Waiting that says rate-limited and resuming on its own, and make the chip a target that opens the job rather than the whole profile.

finding: Two of the nine states have no frame, and one of them is the state the brief names as most likely to be dropped. 'differs' — it landed, and the backend's answer is not what was typed because the church office corrected the same field in between — appears nowhere, on the list or the record. Without it, the only two outcomes the design can express are landed and failed, so a job that landed on a value nobody typed shows as a clean row: Tally asserting a value nobody holds, which is exactly the failure the brief spends a paragraph on. 'orphaned' — the person the edit names is gone upstream — also has no frame, and it is not the same as failed: the honest move there is re-create with the edit riding along, and no frame shows that path. The offline hold ('nothing has left this device yet') is likewise unrepresented, which matters less on a laptop but shares a component with the phone.
evidence: A text sweep of all five desktop prototypes returns no occurrence of differs, changed upstream, no longer exists, re-create, stalled, taking longer, or offline. The vocabulary on the glass is four words total: Saving, Waiting, Needs you, Queued.
direction: 'differs' needs the record, not the list: the same banner slot, in warn rather than danger, showing typed-vs-held side by side and a single move ('keep theirs' / 'send mine again'). It is the one place the 640px column is genuinely the right width, because it is a two-column comparison. 'orphaned' can reuse the failed banner shape with the existing re-create action as its single move.

where: the red banner on the record (y 165–322) and the 'Needs you 1' pill in the filter row
finding: The design answers one failure on one record and has no answer for the failure class the brief singles out. When credentials rotate or write-back is switched off, every queued job fails at once — the brief says the screen must aggregate rather than print it nine times. Here it prints it nine times: nine records each with the same red banner, each offering 'Fix and send again' to a leader who cannot retry their way out of a 401, and a pill that reads 'Needs you 9' without naming a cause or an admin. Priya, arriving next Tuesday knowing only that something failed, can find the single-failure case — the red pill is a real door and it is the right idea — but the pill says 'Needs you', which on a screen already full of incomplete-profile and no-contact language does not say a save was refused, and she still has to open the record to learn what happened and cannot tell a week-old failure from a five-minute-old one from the list.
evidence: sync-failed--desktop-full.png carries the whole story — the field, the quoted reason, 'Marcus Webb', 'last Tuesday', the reassurance that the record still says 14 March 2011 — inside a per-record banner, and nowhere else. The list's only aggregate is the pill count '1'; this page already demonstrates the page-level notice pattern it is missing, in the export strip ('Some of this roster is out of date… could not be reached').
direction: One page-level strip above the list when a whole class of jobs is refused for one reason, naming the reason and the admin once, with the affected count as a filter into the list — and per-record banners suppressed to a short reference while it stands. On the pill, say what needs her ('Saves failed 1') and carry the age of the oldest into the filtered rows so a week-old refusal looks a week old.

where: the whole content column, x 512–1152, and the banner at the top of it
finding: This is a phone layout centred in a laptop, and the new banner is the phone move — a full-bleed strip that pushes the record down. In a 1440×900 window the sidebar takes 224 and the working area is 1216, but the record is a 640px column with 288px of empty page on each side: 47% of the space Dana has is unused, and the answer to that waste is being paid for vertically instead. The banner spends 140px plus its gap — roughly 160px, 18% of the fold — to deliver three facts and one button, and it pushes Edit profile, the whole Profile card and everything under it down by that much. Dana's Tuesday is a session of records with edits in flight, so this is the normal state of the screen, not the exception. The result: the Attendance card, which is why she opened the record at all, starts 973px down a 1532px page and she scrolls for it every time.
evidence: sync-profile--desktop-full.png: card left edge 512, right edge 1152 (640px) inside a 1216px main area; page height 1532 against a 900 fold, so 632px below it. Three sections stacked in one column — Profile (h≈530), Attendance (h≈380), Every gathering (h≈130) — none wider than 640. The amber banner runs y 165–305, and in sync-failed the red one runs y 165–322 and pushes everything a further 20px.
direction: At lg and up let the record be two columns in the 1216 it has: Profile on the left, Attendance and the gathering log on the right, which puts the whole record above the fold. Give the job state the header row rather than a strip of its own — the 576px of gutter beside 'Ava Chen-Ito' is exactly where 'Last name and grade · queued by you · 14s' and its one button belong, at zero vertical cost. Keep the full-bleed strip for the phone; this is a responsive difference, not a compromise.

where: the modal, x 448–992, and its internally scrolling body
finding: The form Dana uses nine times in four minutes is 544px wide in a 1216px working area and still does not fit the window: at 900px tall the modal body clips Status and the Parent contact block behind an internal scroll. So on a laptop with 672px of empty width she scrolls inside a dialog to reach two of the eight controls, and the scroll is inside a box with no visible scrollbar chrome, which is where people conclude a field does not exist. Nine times in four minutes, that is nine internal scrolls to reach a control that could have been in the column beside the one she is typing in.
evidence: sync-editor--desktop-fold.png ends the body at Notes (y≈789) and goes straight to the footer; sync-editor--desktop-full.png shows Status and Parent contact between them, so ~250px of form is behind the scroll. The dialog is sm:max-w-[34rem] = 544px with max-h-[92dvh] = 828px at this window against ~1051px of content. First/Last name already sit side by side, so the two-column idea is present and then abandoned for the remaining six controls.
direction: Widen the dialog at lg and lay the managed fields (name, nickname, grade, birthday) against the Tally-owned ones (notes, status) in two columns, so the whole form is one screen with no internal scroll and the Planning-Center-vs-Tally split becomes spatial instead of a sentence at the top. The phone keeps the single column and the sheet.

where: the amber banner: headline, body sentence, and the 'Undo this edit' button at y 257–289
finding: The banner names two different states for one job and then offers an action that is only valid in one of them. The headline says 'Saving to Planning Center' — a worker is talking to the backend now — and the sentence under it says 'queued by you 14 seconds ago' — nothing has claimed it yet. Those are different rows in the brief's table with different rules, and the button assumes the second: only a queued job is cancellable. If the job is actually sending, pressing Undo cannot stop the patch, and Dana walks away believing the old surname survived when the new one is landing. That is a leader confidently holding the wrong belief about what is in the church's people database, which is the whole thing this refinement is trying to end. 'Undo' is also a word this product has already spent — in check-in it means an instant, certain reversal of a tap — and reusing it for a race is the wrong promise.
evidence: sync-profile--desktop-fold.png, banner text in full: '◷ Saving to Planning Center / Last name and grade, queued by you 14 seconds ago. It carries on without this page — you can close the tab.' with a single primary button 'Undo this edit'. No age threshold, no distinction of the two words, no statement of what happens if it is already out.
direction: Pick one state per render and say it: 'Queued — nothing has left yet' with 'Cancel this edit', or 'Sending to Planning Center' with the cancel gone or explicitly labelled as a request that may not win. If a job in flight can still be pulled back, say what it will do ('stop it if it has not gone out'). Keep 'undo' for check-in.
